# MiniVM

MiniVM is a toy column virtual machine. It runs straight-line programs whose
instructions each operate on whole columns of values, and it reports how many
cycles each run costs.

## Example

```text
LOAD    a, orders.o_amt
GT      m, a, 100.00
IDX     i, m
GATHER  big, a, i
OUT     big
```

- `LOAD` reads the stored column `orders.o_amt` into register `a`.
- `GT` sets `m` to a BOOL column: `a > 100.00` at each row.
- `IDX` sets `i` to the positions where `m` is TRUE.
- `GATHER` sets `big` to the values of `a` at the positions in `i`.
- `OUT` makes `big` the program's result.

Saved as `big.mini`, run it from the bundle root:

```sh
bin/minivm big.mini examples/data.json

# Language

This page gives the syntax of MiniVM programs: lines, comments, opcodes,
registers, operands and literals.

## Programs

A program is straight-line: its instructions run once each, in order. Each
line holds one instruction. A `;` starts a comment, which runs to the end of
the line; a line may hold only a comment, or be blank. Spaces and tabs are
interchangeable: they separate the opcode from its operands, and may indent a
line or surround an operand.

```text
; Ids and amounts of orders over 100.
load   id, orders.o_id
load   amt, orders.o_amt
gt     m, amt, 100      ; NULL where o_amt is NULL
idx    i, m
gather a, id, i
gather b, amt, i
out    a, b
```

The program must end with its only `OUT`; see [Program rules](running.md#program
-rules).                                                                        
## Instructions

An instruction is an opcode followed by comma-separated operands:

```text
OP dest, operand, ...
```

Opcodes are case-insensitive: `gt`, `Gt` and `GT` are the same instruction.
So are the keywords `NULL`, `TRUE`, `FALSE`, `ASC`, `DESC`, `NF`, `NL` and
`NULLEQ`.
Each opcode's operands are given on its page in the
[instruction reference](instructions/README.md).

## Registers

Register names are identifiers, such as `r1`, `amt` or `_t0`: a letter or `_`,
followed by letters, digits and `_`. Register names are case-sensitive, and a
keyword can't be a register name. A register holds a column or a group set
([Values](values.md#columns-and-group-sets)) and can be overwritten.

## Operands

An operand is one of:

| Operand | Example | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| register | `amt` | every instruction |
| literal | `100.00` | element-wise instructions, `FILL`, integer operands such 
as `LEFT`'s `n` |                                                               | `table.column` | `orders.o_amt` | [`LOAD`](instructions/columns.md#load) |
| sort key | `amt DESC NL` | [`SORT`, `TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys)
 |                                                                              | `NULLEQ` | `NULLEQ` | [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) 
|                                                                               
## Literals

| Literal | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `42`, `-7` | INT | must fit in 128 bits |
| `12.50` | NUM | must be exact, in the [NUM range](values.md#num-range) |
| `'it''s'` | STR | a quote inside the string is written twice |
| `#2024-01-31#` | DATE | years 0001 to 9999 |
| `NULL` | NULL | |
| `TRUE`, `FALSE` | BOOL | |

A literal stands for that value at every row.

## Integer operands

Some operands must be integer literals rather than registers: `n` and `len`
(`LEFT`, `SUBSTR`, `SLICE`, `TOPK`) are non-negative, and `SUBSTR`'s `start` is
at least 1. They may be arbitrarily large; a count larger than the input means
all of it.

# Values

This page describes MiniVM's values and types, what a register holds, and how
values are ordered and compared.

## Types

| Type | Values | Literal |
|---|---|---|
| INT | exact 128-bit integer; a result outside -2^127 .. 2^127-1 is an error | 
`42` |                                                                          | NUM | decimal: see [NUM range](#num-range) | `12.50` |
| STR | string | `'it''s'` |
| DATE | calendar date | `#2024-01-31#` |
| BOOL | `FALSE` or `TRUE` | `TRUE` |

`NULL` is a value of its own, written `NULL`. Unless an instruction says
otherwise, an element-wise result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`
([element-wise instructions](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)).

Literal syntax is in [Literals](language.md#literals). Stored columns have
type INT, NUM, STR or DATE ([table sets](running.md#table-sets)).

## NUM range

A NUM is below 1e28 in magnitude and has at most 28 digits after the point,
and its digits without the point, read as an integer, are at most
2^96 - 1 = 79228162514264337593543950335: 28 or 29 significant digits.
A NUM keeps its digits after the point, so `1.0` and `1.00` are equal but
print differently.

A NUM literal or stored value must be such a number exactly; trailing zeros
after the point are dropped as far as needed. A NUM result is rounded half to
even to the most digits after the point that fit, and a result of magnitude
1e28 or more is the error `numeric overflow`. Where an INT meets a NUM in
arithmetic, and in `DIV`, an INT operand above 2^96 - 1 in magnitude is that
error too, even if the result would fit.

## Columns and group sets

A register holds either:

- a **column**: a vector of values; or
- a **group set**: a grouping of rows, made by
  [`GROUP`](instructions/grouping.md#group) or [`GALL`](instructions/grouping.md
#gall)                                                                            and read by the other [grouping instructions](instructions/grouping.md).

Registers can be overwritten.

## Ordering

These instructions compare values:

- [`EQ`, `NE`, `LT`, `LE`, `GT`, `GE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) 
and [`IS`](instructions/logic.md#is)                                            - [`SORT`](instructions/sorting.md#sort) and [`TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#to
pk)                                                                             - the joins [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin)
- [`GMIN`, `GMAX`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax)

They order values as follows:

| Values | Order |
|---|---|
| INT and NUM | by numeric value, exactly at any magnitude; INT and NUM mix |
| STR | by bytes |
| DATE | by date |
| BOOL | `FALSE < TRUE` |

Comparing any other mix of types, such as STR with INT or DATE with NUM, is an
error.

String comparison is exact: there is no case folding, and trailing spaces
count, so `'ab'` and `'ab '` differ, as do `'ab'` and `'AB'`.

How each instruction treats `NULL` is given on its page; for sorts, see
[sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys).

# Running

This page gives the rules every program must follow, what happens on an error,
how to run a program with `bin/minivm`, and the JSON format of the tables it
reads.

## Program rules

The last instruction must be the program's only [`OUT`](instructions/columns.md#
out).                                                                           
| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| instructions per program | at most 20,000 |
| values held by one register | at most 4,000,000 (a join's output counts) |
| values held by all registers together | at most 64,000,000; a long string coun
ts as several values (about 1 per 32 bytes) |                                   | work per run | roughly 300,000,000 [cycles](cycles.md); see below |
| rows per table | at most 10,000 |
| program file | at most 4 MiB |
| table-set file | at most 32 MiB and 2,000,000 JSON values |

The work limit stops runaway programs. It counts a run's cycles, but `HJOIN`
and `GROUP` and copying long strings use it up faster than their cycles
suggest, so such programs stop somewhat sooner. Exceeding it, like any other
limit, is an error. It has no effect on the cycles reported for a run that
finishes.

## Errors

Any error stops the program. No result is printed; the error goes to stderr
and `bin/minivm` exits with status 1.

## Command line

```sh
bin/minivm PROGRAM.mini TABLES.json
bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json
```

runs the program in `PROGRAM.mini` on the [table set](#table-sets) in
`TABLES.json`. On success it prints one line of JSON to stdout and exits 0:

```json
{"ncols": N, "rows": [...], "cycles": C}
```

- `ncols` is the number of `OUT` operands.
- `rows` is the result, one array of `ncols` values per row.
  `NULL` is `null` and a BOOL is `true` or `false`. An INT is a JSON integer,
  or a string of its digits outside -2^63 .. 2^63-1. A NUM is a string that keep
s                                                                                 its digits after the point (`"250.00"`), a STR a string, and a DATE a string
  `"YYYY-MM-DD"`.
- `cycles` is the program's cost ([Cycles](cycles.md)).

| Exit status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | success; the result is on stdout |
| 1 | error; the message is on stderr |
| 2 | wrong number of arguments; a usage line is on stderr |

With the program from [Language](language.md#programs) saved as
`over100.mini` and the [example table set](#example) as `orders.json`:

```sh
$ bin/minivm over100.mini orders.json
{"ncols":2,"rows":[[1,"250.00"]],"cycles":42}
```

`bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` prints the table set's [schema file](#schema-f
iles)                                                                           as one line of JSON instead of running a program.

A program that compares a DATE with an INT stops with an error:

```text
LOAD d, orders.o_date
GT   m, d, 5
OUT  m
```

```sh
$ bin/minivm bad.mini orders.json
error: line 2: GT: expected a number, got DATE
```

## Table sets

A table set is a JSON object mapping each table name to its columns and rows:

```json
{"<table>": {"columns": [{"name": "c", "type": "INT|NUM|STR|DATE"}], "rows": [[.
..], ...]}}                                                                     ```

- Table and column names are identifiers (letters, digits and `_`, not starting
  with a digit), compared without regard to case. Duplicate names are an error.
- `columns` lists each column's `name` and `type`, one of `INT`, `NUM`, `STR`, `
DATE`.                                                                          - `rows` lists each row as an array of values, one per column, in column order.
  A table without `rows` is empty.
- A table may also declare [constraints](#constraints).
- Any key other than those shown or listed there is an error, as is a repeated k
ey.                                                                             - A table holds at most 10,000 rows.
- INT values are JSON integers that fit in 32 bits.
- NUM values may be JSON numbers or strings. They must be exact, in the
  [NUM range](values.md#num-range).
- Dates are strings `"YYYY-MM-DD"`, years 0001 to 9999.
- JSON `null` is `NULL`.

A program reads a stored column with `LOAD d, table.column` ([`LOAD`](instructio
ns/columns.md#load)).

A table may declare what its rows guarantee. `bin/minivm` checks every declared
constraint when it reads the table set, and a table set that breaks one is an er

| Key | Example | Guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | `["l_order", "l_no"]` | the columns are never `NULL`, and no two rows 
agree on all of them |                                                          | `not_null` | `["p_price"]` | the columns are never `NULL` |

# Cycles

This page defines how many cycles a program costs. A program's cost is the sum
of its instructions' costs, and `bin/minivm` reports it as `cycles`
([Running](running.md#command-line)).

## Base cost

Every instruction costs 4, plus the cost given for it in the
[cost table](#cost-table). `OUT` costs only the 4.

A run is stopped with an error if it does too much work; see the
[work limit](running.md#program-rules).

## String bytes

The string bytes of a value are the number of bytes in it if it is a STR, and
0 otherwise (including `NULL`).

An [element-wise instruction](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)
costs, for each element of its result, a base amount plus string bytes:

| Instructions | Base per element |
|---|---|
| `DIV` `IDIV` `MOD` | 6 |
| `TRUNC` `YEAR` `MONTH` `DAY` `DOW` `DATEADD` `DATEDIFF` | 2 |
| every other element-wise instruction | 1 |

| Instructions | String bytes per element |
|---|---|
| comparisons: `EQ` `NE` `LT` `LE` `GT` `GE` `IS` | the bytes of the shorter ope
rand |                                                                          | `LEN` | the bytes of its operand |
| `ISNULL` `NVL` `IF` `NULLIF` `NULLIFE` | nothing |
| every other element-wise instruction | 1 per byte of each string operand (lite
rals included) and of its result |                                              
A literal operand counts at every element, like the value it stands for.

## Comparisons

`SORT` and `TOPK` compare rows on their sort keys
([sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys)). One comparison of two rows
costs, for each key examined until one differs, 2 plus the bytes of the
shorter string.

For example, on a table `t` whose STR column `s` and INT column `n` hold the
rows `('ab', 5)` and `('ab', 7)`, comparing the two rows on keys
`s ASC NL, n ASC NL` costs 2 + 2 for the first key, which is equal, and 2 + 0
for the second, which differs: 6 in all. Sorting the two rows takes that one
comparison:

```text
LOAD s, t.s
LOAD n, t.n
SORT o, s ASC NL, n ASC NL
OUT  o
```

costs (4 + 2) + (4 + 2) + (4 + 2 x 2 rows + 6) + 4 = 30 cycles.

## Example

On a table `t` whose STR column `s` holds `'ab'`, `'cde'`, `NULL`:

```text

OUT   e
```

| Instruction | Cost | Cycles |
|---|---|---|
| `LOAD x, t.s` | 4 + 3 values | 7 |
| `UPPER u, x` | 4 + (1 + 2 + 2) + (1 + 3 + 3) + (1 + 0 + 0) | 17 |
| `EQ e, u, 'AB'` | 4 + (1 + 2) + (1 + 2) + (1 + 0) | 11 |
| `OUT e` | 4 | 4 |
| total | | 39 |

shorter of `u` and the literal `'AB'` at each row. `bin/minivm` prints
`{"ncols":1,"rows":[[true],[false],[null]],"cycles":39}`.

   163|SUB d, a, b
   164|MUL d, a, b

   168|UM, rounded as in [NUM range](../values.md#num-range). A result outside the INT or NUM range is the error `numeric overflow`, as is an INT operand above 2^96 - 1 in magnitude when the other operand is NUM.

   178|n when both operands are INT. It is an error if `b` is 0, and `numeric overflow` if the quotient is outside the NUM range or an INT operand is above 2^96 - 1 in magnitude.

   371|# Grouping instructions
   372|
   373|`GROUP` and `GALL` divide rows into groups and store them as a group set; the ot
   374|her instructions on this page read a group set and return columns. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                           
   375|| Instruction | Result |
   376||---|---|
   377|| [`GROUP g, k, ...`](#group) | group set: rows with equal keys share a group |
   378|| [`GALL g, s`](#gall) | group set: one group holding every row of `s` |
   379|| [`GID d, g`](#gid) | group number of each row |
   380|| [`GFIRST d, g`](#gfirst) | position of each group's first row |
   381|| [`GCOUNT d, g`](#gcount) | rows per group |
   382|| [`GCOUNTV d, g, s`](#gcountv) | non-NULL values of `s` per group |
   383|| [`GSUM d, g, s`](#gsum) | sum of non-NULL values per group |
   384|| [`GMIN d, g, s` / `GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) | least / greatest non-NULL value per gr
   385|oup |                                                                           
   386|## Group sets
   387|
   388|A register holds either a column or a group set ([values](../values.md#columns-a
   389|nd-group-sets)). A group set assigns each of its rows a group number; groups are numbered from 0 in order of first appearance. [`GROUP`](#group) and [`GALL`](#gall) produce a group set. [`GID`](#gid) returns a column with one value per row; the aggregates [`GFIRST`](#gfirst) through [`GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) return a column with one value per group, the value for group `k` at position `k`. The `s` operand of an aggregate is a column over the same rows as the group set; a different length is an error.                                                            
   390|Aggregate columns of the same group set line up with each other. To label each g
   391|roup with its key, gather the key at [`GFIRST`](#gfirst). Orders per status:    
   392|```text
   393|LOAD   st, orders.o_status
   394|GROUP  g, st
   395|GFIRST f, g
   396|GATHER key, st, f
   397|GCOUNT n, g
   398|OUT    key, n
   399|```
   400|
   401|On `examples/data.json` this prints `[["open",7],["closed",12],["shipped",11]]`.
   402|
   403|## `GROUP`
   404|
   405|```text
   406|GROUP g, k, ...
   407|```
   408|
   409|Sets `g` to a group set over the rows of the key columns `k, ...`: rows with equ
   410|al keys share a group, and NULL equals NULL. All key columns must have the same length. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): INT and NUM mix (`1` and `1.00` share a group), and a key column holding values that can't be compared (e.g. STR and INT) is an error.                                       
   411|**Cycles:** per row: 6 plus the string bytes of its keys ([rules](../cycles.md#s
   412|tring-bytes)).                                                                  
   413|## `GALL`
   414|
   415|```text
   416|GALL g, s
   417|```
   418|
   419|Sets `g` to a group set with one group holding every row of `s`, even when `s` i
   420|s empty.                                                                        
   421|**Cycles:** 1 per row.
   422|
   423|## `GID`
   424|
   425|```text
   426|GID d, g
   427|```
   428|
   429|Sets `d` to the group number of each row of `g`.
   430|
   431|**Cycles:** 1 per row.
   432|
   433|## `GFIRST`
   434|
   435|```text
   436|GFIRST d, g
   437|```
   438|
   439|Sets `d` to the position of each group's first row. The result is NULL for the g
   440|roup of an empty `GALL`.                                                        
   441|**Cycles:** 1 per row.
   442|
   443|## `GCOUNT`
   444|
   445|```text
   446|GCOUNT d, g
   447|```
   448|
   449|Sets `d` to the number of rows in each group.
   450|
   451|**Cycles:** 2 per row.
   452|
   453|## `GCOUNTV`
   454|
   455|```text
   456|GCOUNTV d, g, s
   457|```
   458|
   459|Sets `d` to the number of non-NULL values of `s` in each group.
   460|
   461|**Cycles:** 2 per row.
   462|
   463|## `GSUM`
   464|
   465|```text
   466|GSUM d, g, s
   467|```
   468|
   469|Sets `d` to the sum of the non-NULL values of `s` in each group: INT when all ar
   470|e INT, else NUM. The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values. A NUM sum is computed exactly, with as many digits after the point as the value with the most, and rounded once as in [NUM range](../values.md#num-range), so it doesn't depend on the order of the rows. Only each group's total is checked: a total outside the INT or NUM range is the error `numeric overflow`, whatever the running sums along the way.                                                           
   471|**Cycles:** 2 per row.
   472|
   473|## `GMIN`, `GMAX`
   474|
   475|```text
   476|GMIN d, g, s
   477|GMAX d, g, s
   478|```
   479|
   480|Sets `d` to the least (`GMIN`) or greatest (`GMAX`) non-NULL value of `s` in eac
   481|h group, the first of equals: of `1`, `1.0` and `1.00`, whichever comes first. Values are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering). The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values.                                             
   482|**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus the bytes of each non-NULL string ([rules](../cycles
   483|.md#string-bytes)).                                                             [MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Joins

   485|# Join instructions
   486|
   487|`NLJOIN` and `HJOIN` pair up the rows of two key columns whose keys are equal an
   488|d return the pairs as two position columns. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                                                  
   489|| Instruction | Result |
   490||---|---|
   491|| [`NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | positions of all pairs w
   492|ith `lk[i] = rk[j]` |                                                           | [`HJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | same result as `NLJOIN` |
   493|
   494|## `NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`
   495|
   496|```text
   497|NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]
   498|HJOIN  li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]
   499|```
   500|
   501|Finds all pairs `(i, j)` with `lk[i] = rk[j]`, ordered by `i` then `j`. Sets `li
   502|` to the positions into `lk` and `ri` to the positions into `rk`, one entry per pair; if `li` and `ri` are the same register, it holds the positions into `rk`. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): a non-NULL left key that can't be compared with a non-NULL right key (e.g. STR with INT) is an error. A NULL key matches no key, unless the optional `NULLEQ` flag is given, in which case NULL keys match each other. `HJOIN` gives the same result as `NLJOIN`, errors included; only the cost differs.                                            
   503|**Cycles (`NLJOIN`):** per pair of rows: 1 plus the bytes of the shorter string 
   504|key ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.               
   505|**Cycles (`HJOIN`):** per row of either side: 6 plus its key's string bytes ([ru
   506|les](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.                       
   507|### Example
   508|
   509|[`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) through `li` picks columns of the left rows and th
   510|rough `ri` columns of the right rows, giving one row per pair. Customers with their region's name:                                                              
   511|```text
   512|LOAD   reg, customers.c_region
   513|LOAD   code, regions.r_code
   514|HJOIN  li, ri, reg, code
   515|LOAD   cname, customers.c_name
   516|LOAD   rname, regions.r_name
   517|GATHER c, cname, li
   518|GATHER r, rname, ri
   519|OUT    c, r
   520|```
   521|
   522|On `examples/data.json` this prints `[["Cy","Southern"],["Dee","West Coast"],["E
   523|ve","Southern"], ...]`.                                                         [MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Logic

   528| page follow the [element-wise rules](README.md#element-wise-instructions); where an instruction's NULL behavior differs from the default (the result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`), its section says so.

   546|LT d, a, b

   548|GT d, a, b
   549|GE d, a, b

   553|`a >= b`. Values are ordered as described in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering); comparing other mixes of types is an error.

   565|les.md#string-bytes)).

   569|AND d, a, b

   649|# Sorting instructions
   650|
   651|`SORT` and `TOPK` order the rows of one or more key columns and return positions
   652|, which [`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) applies to any column of the same rows. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                
   653|| Instruction | Result |
   654||---|---|
   655|| [`SORT d, key, ...`](#sort) | positions of the rows in stable sorted order |
   656|| [`TOPK d, n, key, ...`](#topk) | the first `n` positions of the same order |
   657|
   658|## `SORT`
   659|
   660|```text
   661|SORT d, key, ...
   662|```
   663|
   664|Sets `d` to the positions of the rows in stable sorted order by the [sort keys](
   665|#sort-keys).                                                                    
   666|**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus every comparison of a stable top-down merge sort ([c
   667|omparison cost](../cycles.md#comparisons)).                                     
   668|## `TOPK`
   669|
   670|```text
   671|TOPK d, n, key, ...
   672|```
   673|
   674|Sets `d` to the first `n` positions of the order `SORT` would produce for the sa
   675|me keys (all of them if there are fewer rows). `n` is an integer literal.       
   676|**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus every comparison of a bounded insertion buffer (each
   677| row is compared with the current `n`-th, then placed by binary search) ([comparison cost](../cycles.md#comparisons)), plus 1 per buffered row shifted.         
   678|## Sort keys
   679|
   680|```text
   681|reg ASC|DESC NF|NL
   682|```
   683|
   684|A sort key is a register followed by a direction and a NULL placement, separated

    58|
    59|Each row: the original program's cost, what made it slow, and what that means for the optimizer.
    60|
    61|| Example | Cycles orig → hand **[M]** | Hidden lesson |
    62||---|---|---|
    63|| q0001 | 13766 → 1703 (8.1×) | 52% of the cycles are CAT and LEFT building a label for rows a later filter throws away. **Order of work matters more than the work itself.** `SORT` on `lines` is a no-op because of the `sorted` constraint. `GE l_qty,1` is always TRUE because of `not_null` + `check`. |
    64|| q0002 | 3617 → 2011 (1.8×) | The self-join's *counted* side must stay unfiltered. Filtering it too is the naive bug (`q0002.naive`, caught on 17 datasets). Only the outer side may shrink. |
    65|| q0003 | 8562 → 2817 (3.0×; 37× on large) | A "count of better rows" self-join is O(n²) per group. A sort plus per-group rank is linear. The HJOIN silently drops NULL and `''`→NULL keys, and the rewrite must reproduce that. |
    66|| q0004 | 18442 → 2179 (8.5×; 47× on large) | 36% of the cycles are GATHER fan-out across 4 joins. A SORT before GALL/GSUM is useless. **`customers` has no key**, so de-duplicating `c_id` is wrong (`q0004.naive`). |
    67|| q0005 | 5518 → 3294 (1.7×) | Join, then sort, then GROUP de-dup is really a **semi-join**. De-duplicate the small side first. |
    68|| q0006 | 6338 → 2091 (3.0×; 20× on large) | A self-join followed by GMAX is GROUP + GMAX + GID. GROUP puts NULLs in one group but HJOIN never matches them, so an explicit NULL filter is required (`q0006.naive`). |
    69|| q0007 | 2596 → 637 (4.1×) | Filter first, then TOPK instead of SORT, then build the label for 5 rows. The example data has only 3 July-2023 orders and no tied amounts, so `TOPK 4` and a flipped tie-break both **passed on the example data**. |
    70|| q0008 | 1524 → 1249 (1.2×) | Already tight. Dead loads are the only waste. Not every legacy program is slow. |

    74|   - The generic wins are filter-first, late materialization, GATHER sinking, dead-code elimination, and TOPK instead of SORT.
    75|   - The self-join idioms give the largest gains on large data, and they are also the riskiest.
